To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the minimum number of markers needed to assign individuals correctly to their continent of origin (i.e., Africa, Europe, or Asia) is 60 Alu insertion polymorphic loci or microsatellites.

1) a minimum of 100 loci is required to assign individuals to continent of origin with a mean accuracy >90% under ideal experimental conditions, 2) a minimum of approximately 200 individuals is required to achieve this level of accuracy, 3) a minimum of at least 60 loci is required for accurate assignment to the appropriate genetic clusters, and 4) proxies such as skin color and self-reported ethnicity are not sufficient and accurate representations for assignment to genetic groups.

(1) a minimum of 100 loci is required to infer population structure at a level of resolution sufficient to distinguish continental origins and (2) the accuracy of assignment to population structure is strongly influenced by the nature of the proxy used to infer membership in these groups.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of identifying the genetic basis of phenotypic differences among groups.
the development of a framework for making inferences on population structure and the validity of proxies.
developing the capability to make strong inclusions about population structure and group membership.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the utility of any given proxy depends on the specific application and the level of population structure being sought, and that proxies should be used with great caution and only after a careful assessment of their accuracy.
the number of loci needed to identify population structure depends on the degree of population structure and the level of resolution desired.
population structure can be resolved to the level of continent of origin and that proxies for genetic clusters are useful, but only if they are carefully chosen and their utility is tested.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a minimum of 100 loci, and preferably 200, are necessary to make accurate inferences of population structure in Old World populations, and that proxies are more useful than skin color in this regard.

the number of markers required to identify population structures is high, that population structure can be resolved at a fine level, and that the accuracy with which proxies represent these structures depends on the proxy and the population of interest.

, in order to make strong inclusions about population structure, it is necessary that the number of markers used be at least 60 and preferably 100, and that the proxies used be carefully selected and their correspondence to the population structure be carefully evaluated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to make accurate inferences, we must use a large number of markers.
the genetic variation underlying the proxies used to define groups may not be sufficient for accurate assignment.
population structure can be inferred with high accuracy from a relatively modest set of genetic markers.
